summary: Defines a human-readable string form for LDAP search filters, which are otherwise sent over the network in a different encoding. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 2254.

plainLanguage.summary: A directory search is normally a compact code that people cannot read. This 1996 document defines a text form that looks like nested brackets, so a person can write and read rules such as what name and class an entry must have. It was later replaced by an extended version.

questions: how to write an ldap search filter
what is the ldap filter string format
how do ldap filter operators work
subtitle: A human-readable format for specifying which directory entries you want.

tldr.problem: LDAP search filters are normally encoded in a binary format for transmission over the network, which is not readable by humans.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1960 defines a plain text format for writing LDAP filters using prefix notation, with logical operators and comparison operators and parentheses around each part.
tldr.outcome: It was obsoleted by RFC 2254, which extended the format.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 1960 as a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1558 and is obsoleted by RFC 2254. The later document extended the string format this one defined.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) defines a network representation of a search filter that a client sends to a directory server. This RFC defines a human-readable string format for those filters, so they can be written and understood by people rather than only transmitted in their encoding.

The string form uses a prefix format: the operator comes first and its arguments follow, all wrapped in parentheses. Logical operators such as & for and and | for or combine other filters, while comparison operators such as = and >= match attribute values.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing code that only computers understand, this format lets you write directory search rules in a way that people can read and write.

sections.title: The Filter Grammar
sections.content:
A filter is a parenthesized expression. The equals operator tests exact matches, approximately-equals tests similarity, greater-or-equal tests whether a value is at least as large, and less-or-equal tests whether it is at most as large. The special form with equals followed by an asterisk tests whether an attribute is present. Substring matching uses asterisks as wildcards in the middle or at the ends of a value.

Logical operators combine filters: & requires all conditions, | requires at least one, and ! negates. If a value must contain an asterisk or a parenthesis, that character is escaped with a backslash. The RFC notes that the construction attr=* is used only to denote a presence filter.
sections.plainLanguage: It works like asking for records with conditions: find people named John with email addresses, or find all Smiths except Tim. The asterisk stands for any characters you do not know.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: Simple equality, (cn=Babs Jensen), matches entries where the common name is exactly Babs Jensen. Negation, (!(cn=Tim Howes)), matches any entry except Tim Howes. A combination such as (&(objectClass=Person)(|(sn=Jensen)(cn=Babs J*))) matches persons whose surname is Jensen or whose common name begins with Babs J. Wildcards in values, such as (o=univ*of*mich*), use asterisks to match any substring.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for people named Babs, or anyone except Tim, or a combination of conditions, and the asterisk lets you match partial words.
